chapter: Connie's Inn, Duke Ellington and the Swingland band
title: Section balance and taping Willie Randall's loud third alto
summary: Third altos usually had the weakest tone; Willie Randall overplayed and drowned lead altoist Simeon until Horace taped the section and let him hear himself.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Right. A natural puts your tenors and trumpets in B natural. Yeah. That would be a problem. Did you -- when you were rehearsing, did you really concentrate a lot on intonation and good sharp cut offs?
Yes. Well, (I knew the individuals in the band, unintelligible)

-- that had the best tone, and the guys that didn't have -- generally, you know, in those days, the third alto had the worst tone, as a general rule, you know. So we'd put him in the middle where his note was important
but yet didn't stand out. And I used to have a little alto player. His name was -- I called it before here -- Willy Randall.

And the only trouble I had with him -- a lot of times we had trouble with him over shouting the five saxophones in the reed section. That third alto is very -- those notes that he has sometimes important, and has to be treated (Unintelligible). So sometime, he would play them so loud that he would make the chord sound like it was a dischord, you know. And I used to tell him, I'd say, 'Willy, you're overshadowing your lead man, first alto player.' I said a chord is supposed to be built like this, like an angle. The first man on top, then there you are, and then there's your tenor, and your tenor support, and then it would sound mellow. I never could get that over to him for a long time, except one time I did exactly what we are doing now, I taped something for him once and played the reed section chorus back, and Willy -- I was hoping that he would play loud like we'd had trouble -- he did. And I played it back, and he heard himself. From that day on, I had trouble with him bringing it out.
That was the greatest teacher, you know. So he said, 'Is that me? Man, that can't be.' I said, 'Well, listen to the notes, Willie.' I said, 'That's you. That

Simeon. " Simeon's isn't Simeon. Simeon's the lead alto player. He says, "Now I hear, I see how bad I sounded." It was fun. We made that thing, man, and we made jokes out of everything. Nobody got mad, you know, but it was a constructive criticism, you know, so it worked out real fine. And I got so I could get that mellowness that I wanted, you know, in the section.
